## Fixed-block logarithmic rate abstraction (2026-10-22)

The abstraction search used Mathlib's official
[`Analysis.Asymptotics.ExpGrowth` API](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Analysis/Asymptotics/ExpGrowth.html)
and checked its source at the repository-pinned Mathlib revision
`380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51`. Mathlib defines
`ExpGrowth.expGrowthSup p = \limsup_n \log(p_n)/n` and provides
`ExpGrowth.expGrowthSup_le_iff` for eventual exponential upper bounds. This
is the standard abstract exponential-growth interface, but its normalization
is the fixed index `n`; it does not directly express the varying block-count
normalization used in the small-deviation arguments.

The stable-process block proof and the Brownian finite-cover proof both use
the same implication: if $p_n\le q^{m_n}$ eventually, $r_n\ge0$ eventually,
$r_nm_n\to c$, and $p_n>0$ eventually, then
\[
  \limsup_n r_n\log p_n\le c\log q,
\]
provided the real-valued logarithmic sequence is lower-cobounded. That
shared statement is now
`ProbabilityTheory.limsup_probabilityRate_le_of_eventually_le_pow` in
`Probability/MeasureTheory/Asymptotics/LogarithmicRate.lean`, alongside
the existing finite-product lower-rate statement. The two random-walk files
retain the event-specific block estimates and prove their respective limits
for $r_nm_n$.

The finite-cover parameter file had two further declarations used only by
its own parameter-selection proof. They are now `private`; the cross-module
selection result remains under `Spectral/Range/Rate/Lemmas/`, where its
proof-specific role is visible. This audit follows the abstract API already
present in Mathlib while introducing only the additional variable-rate
statement required by both clients.

## Ordered child-slot prefix abstraction review (2026-10-22)

The search compared the ordered-slot API with Mathlib's official
[`Finset.Iio` and `Finset.mem_Iio` definitions](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Order/Interval/Finset/Defs.html#Finset.Iio)
and the pinned source at revision
`380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51`. Mathlib defines `Finset.Iio a`
for `[Preorder α] [LocallyFiniteOrderBot α]`, with
`x ∈ Finset.Iio a ↔ x < a`; this is the generic finite strict initial interval
and is the right representation for the first `N` child slots. Accordingly,
`firstSlots α N` now uses
`Finset.Iio ((slotOrderIsoNat α).symm N)` instead of mapping
`Finset.range N` through the inverse order isomorphism. The existing
membership and cardinality theorems verify that this interval contains
exactly the slots of rank below `N` and has cardinality `N`.

The Mathlib source module
[`Order/SuccPred/LinearLocallyFinite.lean`](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51/Mathlib/Order/SuccPred/LinearLocallyFinite.lean)
provides `orderIsoNatOfLinearSuccPredArch` under successor, predecessor, and
successor-Archimedean structures, as well as the derivation of those
structures from a linear locally finite order. `slotOrderIsoNat` packages
that derivation with the actual child-slot assumptions
`[LinearOrder α] [LocallyFiniteOrder α] [OrderBot α] [NoMaxOrder α]`, yielding
the canonical rank `e : α ≃o ℕ` without requiring clients to install the
internal successor/predecessor structures. This is the ordered-slot ranking
interface, while `firstSlots` uses Mathlib's already-generic interval
operation; no separate general-purpose prefix or interval abstraction was
added.

The former `Step/Measure/Potential.lean` bundled two semantic layers: the

ordered after mapping its marks through that potential. The latter depended
on `Ordering/Monotone`, while measure-weight interfaces depended on the same
file. The declarations are now split by owner: `Step/Potential.lean` contains
measurable real-valued mark observations, additive potentials, their path-sum
operations, and coordinate measurability; `Step/Ordering/ByPotential.lean`
contains `Step.IsOrderedBy`, `orderedBySteps`, its membership law, and the
measurability theorem. Thus `Measure/ExponentialWeight.lean` imports only the
base observation interface, while ordering realizations import the ordering
adapter.

The abstraction check used Mathlib's official documentation for
[`Measurable`](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/MeasurableSpace/Defs.html),
[`SimpleFunc`](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Function/SimpleFunc.html),
and [`MeasurableEmbedding` / `MeasurableEquiv`](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/MeasurableSpace/Embedding.html),
then inspected the pinned Mathlib source at revision
`380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51`. Mathlib's `Measurable f` is a
proposition on an ordinary function; `SimpleFunc` additionally requires
finite range; and measurable embeddings/equivalences require injectivity or a
measurable inverse. None represents an arbitrary many-to-one measurable mark
observation `X → ℝ`. The local `Potential X` bundle therefore records a
reusable domain concept, while its codomain remains `ℝ` because path addition,
ordering, and exponential weights all consume real values. Making the target
arbitrary would add parameters and operations without a client for them.
Likewise, `AdditivePotential X` is kept as the measurable additive
specialization, backed by Mathlib's existing `AddMonoidHom` rather than a new
generic measurable-hom abstraction. No new generic wrapper is introduced.

This review moves the base potential out of `Measure/` and keeps potential
ordering under `Ordering/`, matching both the dependency direction and the
mathematical ownership. The affected modules are checked with the pinned Lean
build; no LaTeX source is changed in this pass.

## Stable clock-process abstraction review (2026-10-22)

This review inspected `Probability/Process/Stable/{Basic,Process,Levy,
FiniteDimensional}.lean` and `Stable/PathLaw/Basic.lean`, together with their
call sites in stable small-deviation, path-law, Brownian, and Poisson-model
modules. The network comparison used Mathlib's official
[`HasIndepIncrements` documentation](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Probability/Independence/Process/HasIndepIncrements/Basic.html)
and
[`IsPreBrownianReal` documentation](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Probability/BrownianMotion/Basic.html),
then verified the dependency interfaces in the pinned Mathlib source at
`380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51`. The independent comparison
formalization `slink/LeanLevy`, revision
`7e73fd9b23ad52956ec2756a815889a783131ce4`, defines `IsLevyProcess` by a
zero start, independent and stationary increments, and almost-surely càdlàg
paths; its stochastic-process module identifies its independent-increment
predicate with Mathlib's. This project is cited as a design comparison, not
used as a dependency.

The source comparison supports the current division of responsibility:
Mathlib's `HasIndepIncrements X P` already states mutual independence of
successive differences along every finite monotone time grid. Mathlib's
`IsPreBrownianReal` is the Brownian-specific finite-dimensional-law interface,
so it does not express the stable, generally non-Gaussian increment laws or a
deterministic time-change clock. Locally,
`HasStableClockIncrements α μ clock X P` adds exactly that missing
specification: `μ` is strictly `α`-stable, `clock` is monotone and zero at the
least time, the process starts there almost surely, and
`X_t - X_s` has law
`μ.map (fun x => (clock t - clock s) ^ (1 / α) * x)` for `s ≤ t`. The
independence field reuses Mathlib directly. `IsStableClockProcess` adds
almost-sure càdlàg paths, `IsStableLevyProcess` specializes the clock to
identity time on `ℝ≥0`, and `IsStableClockProcessLaw` applies the same
specification to canonical càdlàg paths. The specialization theorem
`IsStableLevyProcess.toIsLevyProcess` connects this stable interface to the
repository's general Lévy-process definition.

An additional public `HasIncrementLaw` wrapper, or a generic process bundle
for arbitrary indexed increment distributions, would only repackage a family
of `HasLaw` assumptions at present. The generic finite-dimensional results in
`Probability/Process/IndepIncrements/FiniteDimensional.lean` already accept
matching one-step increment laws directly, while the stable clock operations
need the stable scaling formula itself. No additional generic wrapper or
outward move is justified by the inspected uses. The stable-clock definitions
remain under `Probability/Process/Stable`, their path-law form remains beside
the path-space representation, and no theorem-specific proof helper is
promoted.

## Finite-horizon kernel survival interfaces (2026-10-22)

`Probability/Kernel/Survival/` has six direct modules, each exposing a complete

remaining mass and Chapman--Kolmogorov bounds; `Return.lean` restricts block
endpoints to a measurable return set; `VariableBlocks.lean` composes a finite

different measurable target; `Blocking.lean` converts uniform one-block
bounds to arbitrary horizons; and `SubEigenfunction.lean` iterates

single theorem's private proof chain, so they remain outside `Lemmas/`.

The abstraction check compared the exact operations with Mathlib's official
[`Kernel.comapRight` API](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Probability/Kernel/Basic.html)
and [kernel composition and powers](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Probability/Kernel/Composition/Comp.html),

`380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51`. Mathlib supplies target-subtype

identity. `returnKernel` and `bridgeKernel` compose those operations into
finite-horizon kernels whose source and terminal sets are explicit in their

## Finite integer-family range translation (2026-10-22)

The Rademacher integer-coordinate and finite oscillation declarations were
moved from `Mogulskii/Spectral/Range/Basic.lean` to
`RandomWalk/Rademacher/FiniteInterval/Range/Basic.lean`, beside the killed
finite-interval path interface. The Mogulskii spectral `Range/` subtree then
contained the finite-cover and Donsker/spectral estimates that used those
coordinates; subsequent ownership review moved finite-time Rademacher range
and corridor estimates beside the finite-interval walk, and the general block
Donsker comparison to the general random-walk range owner.

The path-cover proof had a model-specific theorem that placed a Rademacher
path in one of $w+1$ translated copies of $[0,w]$. Inspection showed the
underlying fact only needs a finite nonempty family of integers with pairwise
distance at most $w$. It is now the public order-theoretic result
`Order.Bounds.exists_int_translate_into_Icc_of_pairwise_dist_le`:
\[
  \bigl(\forall i,j,\ |x_i-x_j|\le w\bigr)
  \Longrightarrow
  \exists c\in\mathbb Z,\ \forall i,\ c+x_i\in[0,w].
\]
The Rademacher bridge from its real partial sums to this theorem is private
inside `Rademacher/FiniteInterval/Range/Probability.lean`, because it is the only
consumer of the path-specific shift statement.

The abstraction search checked the official Mathlib
[`Finset.exists_min_image`](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Data/Finset/Max.html),
[integer intervals](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Data/Int/Interval.html),
and [order intervals](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Order/Interval/Basic.html),
then verified the pinned Mathlib source at revision
`380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51`. Mathlib supplies the finite
minimum and interval infrastructure but no finite-family translation
theorem, so the new declaration belongs at `Order/Bounds` and introduces no
Rademacher or probability assumptions.

## Mogulskii theorem-entry abstraction review (2026-10-22)

The abstraction question was checked against the official Mathlib
[PR review guidance](https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/pr-review.html#location-location),
the pinned Mathlib source at revision
`380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51`, and A. A. Mogul'skii's original
[1974 article record and full text](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/tvp3978),
alongside the [English translation, DOI 10.1137/1119081](https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/1119081).
The article studies small-deviation probabilities for random-walk sample
paths in `D(0,1)` under stable-domain assumptions. The pinned Mathlib source
has no large-deviation-principle or rate-function interface that states these
probability asymptotics; its available probability, measure-convergence, and
path-space APIs supply ingredients rather than a competing Mogulskii API.

The current theorem entry exposes the article's proved Lean interfaces for
Theorems 1--3. Their distinct source objects and normalizations remain visible:
the discrete walk in the stable domain, the strictly stable process under
space scaling, and the finite-variance walk under Mogulskii scaling. The
article's Theorem 4 concerns a continuous-time source process and remains an
explicit open formalization obligation. Combining these into one generic
statement would require a new LDP/rate-function structure spanning the
random-walk and process path spaces, the source-specific scale hypotheses,
and the finite-corridor energy approximation. There is no second independent
client for that structure in the repository, and it would obscure the
different conclusions instead of expressing a shared operation.

Reusable parts already have lower-level semantic owners: the stable-process
escape-rate interface and its corridor-approximation theorem live with stable
processes; the discrete path-class rate and its normal-domain and
finite-variance specializations live with random walks; and the variable-rate
logarithmic estimates live in `Probability/MeasureTheory/Asymptotics/`.
The exact theorem statements remain in those modules, while
`Mogulskii/Theorems.lean` remains the discoverable import entry for the
article's principal results. No additional universal LDP wrapper or
Mogulskii-specific duplicate abstraction is introduced. This review follows
Mathlib's recommendation to prefer an existing more general API only when it
captures the same mathematical operation with appropriate assumptions, rather
than generalizing a declaration solely because several modules use it.

## Horizontal-tube block abstraction review (2026-10-23)

The three modules under `RandomWalk/SmallDeviation/HorizontalTube/Blocks/`
were compared with Mathlib's official
[conditional-expectation API](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Function/ConditionalExpectation/Basic.html)
and with its pinned source at revision
`380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51`. Mathlib supplies conditional
expectations and the integral identity on measurable past events. The
candidate `MeasureTheory.condExp` with `MeasureTheory.setIntegral_condExp`
provides the measure-theoretic primitives. The local general theorem
`ProbabilityTheory.measureReal_initialInterConditionalBlockIntersection_ge_mul_prod_prefix`
in `Probability/Process/Filtration/ConditionalBlocks.lean` states that if
$A\in\mathcal F_0$, each $E_j\in\mathcal F_{j+1}$, $p_j\ge0$, and
$p_j\le\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_{E_j}\mid\mathcal F_j]$ almost everywhere on
$A\cap\bigcap_{i<j}E_i$, then
\[
  \mathbb P(A)\prod_{j<q}p_j
  \le \mathbb P\!\left(A\cap\bigcap_{j<q}E_j\right).
\]
It is the lowest generic layer needed for the tube argument.

`Blocks/EventBridge.lean` defines the past-dependent finite horizontal-tube
event and identifies its conditional probability with the translated
zero-start endpoint-window probability for arbitrary IID increment laws.
Its central candidate statement is
`iidSequenceLaw_condExp_tubeBlockPairEvent_ge`: a translated zero-start
endpoint-window probability lower bound supplies the conditional bound for a
block after any past position in the tube. `Blocks/Product.lean` exposes
`measureReal_tubeBlockIntersection_ge_prod`, the specialization of the
generic filtration product theorem to these tube events.
`Blocks/Geometry.lean` exposes
`measureReal_tubeBlockIntersection_ge_prod_of_endpointWindows`, which
packages the endpoint-window containment that supplies each next block's
starting-point condition. These are complete horizontal-tube operations with
no finite-variance or Mogulskii-scale assumption, so they remain outside
`Lemmas/` at their semantic owner. The bin selection, narrowed widths, and
finite-variance rate assembly used only for Chapter 3, Lemma 3.5 remain under
`DriftedTube/FiniteVarianceLower/Lemmas/Staircase/`; its `Blocks/Assembly.lean`
consumes the reusable tube interface. No additional general wrapper is needed:
the abstraction boundary is the filtration product theorem together with the
horizontal-tube event semantics and geometry supplied by the local modules.

## Brownian first-window abstraction and proof ownership review (2026-10-23)

The candidate generic representation is the running-minimum characterization
already proved in
`Probability/Process/Path/AboveStart/FirstWindow/Time/RunningMinimum.lean`:
`firstNonnegativeWindowStartUpTo_eq_coe_iff_runningMinimum` states, for a
continuous path $f$, horizon $s$, and finite time $t$, that $T^s(f)=t$ iff
$t+1\le s$, the running minimum is constant from $t$ to $t+1$, and no earlier
admissible unit interval has that property. This uses only continuity of the
path, so it is more general than a Brownian-specific definition. A separate
sliding-window process would restate the same condition and is not added.

Writing $m_f(v)=\min_{0\le r\le v}f(r)$, the exact candidate statement is
\[
T^s(f)=t\iff t+1\le s\ \land\ m_f(t+1)=m_f(t)\ \land\
\forall u,\ (u+1\le s\land m_f(u+1)=m_f(u))\Rightarrow t\le u.
\]

The alternative Mathlib candidate was `MeasureTheory.hittingBtwn` in
`Mathlib/Probability/Process/HittingTime.lean`. The official documentation
specifies first entry of a process into a state-space set and proves its
stopping-time property for discrete adapted processes. It does not package the
future-window condition $f(t+u)\ge f(t)$ for every $u\in[0,1]$; that condition
is not a first state-space hit of the original path process. Mathlib's
`IsBrownianReal.shift` and scaling APIs already cover the standard Brownian
invariances: for fixed $t_0$, the shifted process
$u\mapsto B(t_0+u)-B(t_0)$ is Brownian. Those APIs do not provide the
first-window functional or its continuity theorem. The local layer therefore
keeps the path functional and Brownian-specific distributional consequences.
This comparison used
Mathlib revision `380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51` and
BrownianMotion revision `d6d901b6df592a543b7edf221f92d2ee6760d18d`, checked
against the official [`HittingTime` documentation](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Probability/Process/HittingTime.html)
and [`BrownianMotion.Basic` documentation](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Probability/BrownianMotion/Basic.html).
The source theorem family is Bolthausen, “On a Functional Central Limit
Theorem for Random Walks Conditioned to Stay Positive,” Lemmas 2.2--2.5 and
Theorem 3.2, DOI 10.1214/aop/1176996098.

The Brownian modules now reflect this boundary. The fixed-time statement
$\mathbb P(B_t-m_B(t)>0)=1$ for $t>0$ is a parameterized Brownian path
property, so it lives in `Brownian/Reflection/Path/AboveRunningMinimum.lean`.
The fixed-unit existence estimates, the last-cutoff atom, and the interior and
endpoint return nullity statements depend on the first-window construction
and only support its continuity proof; they live under
`Brownian/AboveStart/FirstWindow/Lemmas/` and their entry modules import them
ordinarily. The pathwise endpoint-return/hitting-time implication remains as
a separate complete result at `FirstWindow/EndpointHittingTime.lean`; it
states an independent consequence for every qualifying endpoint return.

The generic path modules now separate the running-minimum characterization
from endpoint-return consequences. `Path/AboveStart/FirstWindow/Time/RunningMinimum.lean`
contains the core deterministic identities. The path-level first-window
directory groups time-functional results under `Time/` (continuity,
finite-horizon restriction, and probability exhaustion), path transforms under
`Shift/` (uncentered and centered, whole-path and finite-horizon), and the
complete pathwise endpoint-return and descending-hitting-time results under
`EndpointReturn/Basic.lean`. The two rational-time covering steps used only by
the Brownian repeated-minimum nullity proof are under
`EndpointReturn/Lemmas/RationalCover.lean`. The local single-use equivalence
and endpoint-return case split are private inside the pathwise endpoint-return
module; the cutoff proof derives its two-line running-minimum consequence
directly rather than exporting another wrapper. This grouping follows
Mathlib's location guidance to split files when results cover distinct topics
and to place declarations in files matching their scope; see the official
[pull request review guide](https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/pr-review.html#location-location).

## Gaussian escape-scale abstraction review (2026-10-23)

The fixed sequence $n^{1/4}$ in
`Mogulskii/Gaussian/EscapeConstant.lean` was compared with the general
scale representation and with the cited theorem. The repository already has
the abstract predicate `Asymptotics.IsSmallDeviationScale`, together with
`Asymptotics.isSmallDeviationScale_natCast_rpow_of_lt` in
`Analysis/Asymptotics/Scale/Power/SmallDeviation.lean`: for every
$0<p<q$, $n^p\to\infty$ and $n^p/n^q\to0$. Since
`IsMogulskiiScale` is the specialization $q=1/2$, the proof now derives its
$n^{1/4}$ witness by applying this power-scale theorem at
$(p,q)=(1/4,1/2)$ and rewriting square roots as real powers. It does not
introduce a second scale predicate or repeat the limit proof.

At the time of this review, the named $n^{1/4}$ witness served four Gaussian
path-rate constructions and a transparent normal-domain constructor. Later
refactoring removed those exposed dependencies. As of the 2026-10-29 audit, the
explicit exponent is needed only in the Gaussian escape-coefficient proof, so
the witness is derived locally from the general power-scale theorem and the
separate `Mogulskii/Scale/Canonical.lean` module has been removed.

The coefficient being calibrated is the exponent-two specialization of the
stable-process path-law escape rate already defined by
`HasStableProcessEscapeRate`; its conclusion is the Brownian coefficient
$-\pi^2/8$ for the range-diameter tube. Mogul'skii's Theorem 3 gives this
Gaussian specialization in the original article, A. A. Mogul'skii, “Small
deviations in the sample function space,” *Teoriya Veroyatnostei i ee
Primeneniya* 19(4) (1974), 755--765, [English translation, DOI
10.1137/1119081](https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/1119081); the primary
[MathNet record](https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/tvp3978) confirms the source
scope and publication data. The pinned Mathlib APIs checked here provide the
Brownian process and probability-measure structures, but no small-deviation
rate or Brownian range-tube constant. Mathlib's online
[review guidance](https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/pr-review.html#location-location)
recommends checking for a more general existing result and locating a
formalized literature theorem with its mathematical owner. The local path-law
escape-rate predicate is that general representation; no second
`BrownianEscapeConstant` type or alias is needed. The coefficient proof stays
with the Mogulskii Gaussian derivation because its argument calibrates the
path-law limit through the Rademacher tube asymptotic and the finite-interval
spectral estimate.

## Fixed-interval survival decay module boundary (2026-10-23)

The module
RandomWalk/Rademacher/FiniteInterval/Spectral/Survival/Decay.lean groups
the two complete fixed-width rate statements: the logarithmic rate of the
killed-kernel row sum and its corresponding Rademacher survival probability.
They share the same limit and differ by the matrix-to-path probability
identity, so the file represents one mathematical endpoint rather than one
file per declaration. A local estimate used only to prove either endpoint
belongs in its defining module or its Lemmas/ subtree.

This boundary follows Mathlib's subject-oriented module pattern: for example,
Analysis/SpecificLimits/Basic.lean groups several power and geometric-limit
results, while the contributor guide describes single-lemma additions to
existing theories as routine. Thus a standalone file is justified by a
coherent mathematical interface, not by a declaration being called a lemma.
See [Mathlib's contribution guide](https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/how-to-contribute.html)
and the [specific-limits module](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Analysis/SpecificLimits/Basic.html).

## Generic block-corridor second-moment estimate ownership (2026-10-23)

The one-block estimate in Mogulskii/Path/CorridorApproximation.lean had no
Mogulskii-scale hypothesis: it combined the distribution-free margin
inclusion from RandomWalk/Path/Block/Corridor/Core.lean with the block maximal
inequality. Its assumptions were generalized from unit second moment to
centered square-integrable IID increments. The resulting bound is
P(start margin) ≤ P(full block corridor) +
ofReal((length + 1) * variance(id, ν) / radius²). It now lives in
RandomWalk/Path/Block/Corridor/SecondMoment.lean, where the probability and
path event are owned. The Mogulskii module retains only the asymptotic version
that uses its scale and diffusive block length; the old Mogulskii declaration
name was removed without an alias.

This is a single-result module because it owns a complete probability
inequality with a distinct finite-variance assumption and import boundary;
folding it into `Core.lean` would make the distribution-free layer depend on
the maximal-moment API. Mathlib does not prescribe one file per theorem: its
style guide asks module docstrings to state the file's content and main
results, and `Probability/Martingale/OptionalStopping.lean` groups several
related theorems. Here the result is kept outside `Lemmas/` because its
variance-sensitive bound is a reusable interface for any IID block corridor,
not merely a proof step for the Mogulskii application. See the
[Mathlib style guide](https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/style.html#module-docstrings)
and the [OptionalStopping module](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Probability/Martingale/OptionalStopping.html).

The abstraction check compared the pinned Mathlib revision
380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51 at
Vendor/Mathlib/Mathlib/Probability/Martingale/OptionalStopping.lean with the
[official documentation](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Probability/Martingale/OptionalStopping.html).
Mathlib provides Doob's maximal inequality for nonnegative submartingales,
while the repository already provides the centered-IID block-sum maximal
bound; neither supplies this path-corridor probability comparison. The new
result composes those two existing interfaces and adds no narrower generic
wrapper. The module was then generalized to arbitrary centered square-integrable
increment laws, using the variance already present in the block maximal bound.
The updated module builds successfully (3,153 Lake jobs), and the import-boundary
checker passes all 10 public entries with 828 graph visits.

## Strict-interior rate scale positivity (2026-10-23)

`IsMogulskiiScale` gives eventual positivity because its spatial scale tends
to infinity. The two public strict-interior lower-rate theorems in
`Rate/Bounds/Interior.lean` conclude a `liminf`, so positivity at finitely
many initial indices is immaterial. Their former `∀ n, 0 < scale n` premise
was stronger than the stated scale predicate. The proof now uses
`max 1 (scale n)`, which is positive everywhere and eventually equals the
original scale; eventual equality preserves the scale predicate and the
`liminf` expression. The all-positive implementation is private, while the
public interfaces require only `IsMogulskiiScale`. The module builds
successfully (3,432 Lake jobs). At that review point, the generic return-kernel
iteration and its Mogulskii rate consumer still carried pointwise
scale-positivity premises; a subsequent assumption review removed those
premises as recorded below.

## Eventual positivity in killed return iteration (2026-10-23)

The three public bounds in `Kernel/Killed/Return/Uniform.lean` conclude
eventually, so the normalized-coordinate argument only uses `0 < scale i` at
indices where the one-block return estimate is available. The former input
`∀ i, 0 < scale i` has been replaced by the eventual input
`∀ᶠ i, ∃ hscale : 0 < scale i, blockBound i hscale`. This keeps the dependent
scaled-interval witness available to the proof while allowing arbitrary scale
values outside the eventual set. The arbitrary-duration iteration also keeps
its natural eventual block-length premise.

The two public Mogulskii return-rate bounds in `Rate/Bounds/Lower.lean` now
carry that same eventual positive-scale witness with their eventual block
estimate and no longer take an everywhere-positive sequence as a separate

`Rate/Partition/Finite.lean` still forms an everywhere-positive representative
inside its proof because the Gaussian partition `liminf` evaluates scaled
interval subtypes at every index; the representative is eventually equal to

## Bolthausen first-window proof-support ownership (2026-10-24)

Reviewed the four modules under
`Probability/Process/Brownian/AboveStart/FirstWindow/Lemmas/` together with
`Probability/Process/Path/AboveStart/FirstWindow/EndpointReturn/Lemmas/RationalCover.lean`.
The Brownian modules implement distinct steps of Bolthausen's Lemma 2.3:
`Existence.lean` derives a positive interval from independent Gaussian
increments, `CutoffBoundary.lean` removes the last admissible start time,
`InteriorReturn.lean` excludes returns inside the first window, and
`EndpointReturn.lean` excludes a return at its endpoint. Their public
first-window interfaces remain in the sibling semantic modules, including
`FirstWindow/Basic.lean` and `FirstWindow/Continuity.lean`; these proof stages
stay under `Lemmas/` rather than appearing as additional entry points.

`RationalCover.lean` groups the two deterministic path inclusions used by
`InteriorReturn.lean`: a first-window interior return and three running-minimum
contacts each yield the same rational-interval event. The file depends on the
first-window and running-minimum path semantics, while its conclusions serve
the countable-cover argument in Bolthausen's Lemma 2.3. Keeping this pair in a
single `EndpointReturn/Lemmas/` module gives the Brownian argument a generic
path-level proof dependency without exposing it as a standalone reusable API.
The theorem-specific intermediate event remains in the proof-support layer.

The online Mathlib API documentation for
[`Mathlib.Probability.BrownianMotion.Basic`](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Probability/BrownianMotion/Basic.html)
and the pinned source provide Brownian finite-dimensional laws, Gaussian and
independent-increment properties, shifts, scaling, and continuity. They do
not provide this first-window event or its rational running-minimum cover.
The proofs use those general Brownian interfaces directly; no parallel
Brownian-law abstraction is needed for these local steps.

selected from past information, but the filename did not identify that
mathematical operation. It is now `Probability/Independence/AdaptiveChoice.lean`;
the declaration names and namespaces are unchanged, and no old-path alias is
kept. The binary theorem now represents the two past cells `U ∩ S` and
`U ∩ Sᶜ` as a `Bool`-indexed finite family and invokes
`measure_finiteAdaptiveChoice_ge_mul`. This removes its repeated null-
measurability, independence-factorization, and finite-union argument while
preserving the theorem statement. The three theorem declarations and their
formulas are listed in the module header.

remains public in `Probability/Independence/AdaptiveChoice`. The finite
partition estimate is used only in its proof and is now an ordinary import;
Mathlib's `IndepFun.measure_inter_preimage_eq_mul` supplies the per-cell
factorization, while the pinned Mathlib source has no theorem combining that
factorization with an adaptive finite family. The official
[Mathlib independence API documentation](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Probability/Independence/Basic.html)
records the independent-family and product-law interfaces used here. The
corridor feedback client imports the renamed module and builds with it; both

The corridor client uses the adaptive-choice declarations only inside theorem
proofs, so `Probability.Process.Path.Skorokhod.Corridor.UniformBlocks.Feedback.Probability`
imports `Probability.Independence.AdaptiveChoice` ordinarily. Both modules

## Finite observations for independent-increment processes (2026-10-24)

The independent-increment directory had seven direct Lean modules, four of
which formed one finite-observation proof family: sorting an arbitrary finite
time set, building increment and position vectors on that grid, and passing
from finite-dimensional independence to independence of path-valued random
variables. Those modules now live under
`Probability/Process/IndepIncrements/FiniteObservations/`, leaving the root
directory for the time-change, separated-increment, and finite-dimensional-law
interfaces. This groups related results while keeping the finite-observation
theorems discoverable by their mathematical objects.

The review compared the implementation with the pinned Mathlib API. Mathlib's
[`HasIndepIncrements` definition](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Probability/Independence/Process/HasIndepIncrements/Basic.html)
already provides mutual independence along every monotone finite time grid.
Mathlib's [`Finset.orderEmbOfFin`](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Data/Finset/Sort.html)
already supplies the canonical increasing enumeration and its order and range
properties. The public `Grid` module therefore retains only the grid
construction in the `Fin (card - 1 + 1)` indexing required by the increment
definition and its mutual-independence theorem. The one-use order and inverse
index facts used by block paths are in `FiniteObservations/Lemmas/Grid`; unused
strict-order and range wrappers were removed in favor of Mathlib's existing
API.

`BlockVectors` retains the public finite partial-sum object and the three
independence theorems for arbitrary disjoint increment sets, adjacent
partial-sum blocks, and adjacent position vectors. Its measurability and
telescoping facts are private because they serve only the proofs in that
module. `BlockPaths` now exposes only
`HasIndepIncrements.indepFun_finiteObservationQueries`; its sorted-grid
extension, query-index construction, projection measurability, and intermediate
independence theorems are private to the defining module. `DisjointPaths`
retains the three distinct public results for finite query vectors,
function-valued adjacent paths, and mutually independent paths on a finite
sequence of adjacent intervals. Proof-only local imports of `BlockPaths`,
`BlockVectors`, and `Probability.Independence.FiniteFamily` are ordinary imports;
Mathlib dependencies appearing in public statement types remain public.

The moved modules and their dependent callers pass the full package build
(`lake -Kjobs=2 build`, 5,626 jobs). The import-boundary check passes its 10
configured public entries and 830 graph visits. The style linter passes all
1,515 production modules, and the module-header check confirms that each
module in this family lists every module-visible declaration. The repository
currently has no same-stem source-file/directory collisions and no directory
with more than seven direct Lean files.

## Endpoint estimate and power-budget ownership (2026-10-24)

`EndpointDeviation/Rate/Raw.lean` contained only an input-bound wrapper for
the finite-horizon selected-endpoint decomposition. Its only imports were
`Rate/LogScales.lean` and `Endpoint/Sequence/Sublevel.lean`, and neither used

wrapper now sits beside the decomposition in `Endpoint/Basic.lean`, where its
meaning and hypotheses are visible together. `Sublevel.lean` imports
`Endpoint/Basic` directly, `LogScales.lean` has no dependency on the endpoint
decomposition, and the standalone `Rate/Raw.lean` module was removed. The
polynomial conversion theorem is named for its actual input, a supplied
finite-horizon estimate. The remaining logarithmic-scale module was the only
file under `Rate/`; it now lives at `Endpoint/Sequence/LogarithmicScales.lean`,
and its formerly `RawRate`-named parameter results are named for the endpoint
rate they support.

The power estimate formerly placed in the N-selection `Rate/PowerBudget`
module now has the real-sequence statement
`Asymptotics.eventually_floor_rpow_mul_ge`: given $x_n\to\infty$,
$a>0$, $\delta<a+r$, and eventually $x_n^r\le y_n$, it proves
$Cx_n^\delta\le\lfloor x_n^a\rfloor y_n$ eventually, for any real $C$.
The first- and second-stage clients instantiate $y_n=(p_n).toReal$ and
$C=4$. The theorem itself has no probability or branching assumptions and
lives in `Analysis/Asymptotics/Power/FloorProduct.lean`.

The abstraction review checked Mathlib at pinned revision
`380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51`. Its
`tendsto_nat_floor_div_atTop` states
$\lfloor x\rfloor/x\to1$ as $x\to\infty$ with no extra hypothesis, and
`tendsto_rpow_atTop` states $x^s\to\infty$ for $s>0$. These are the two
analytic ingredients, but neither includes the product with a second sequence
or an exponent budget ([pinned floor source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51/Mathlib/Analysis/SpecificLimits/Basic.lean#L740),
[pinned power source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51/Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/Pow/Asymptotics.lean#L38),
[official floor documentation](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Analysis/SpecificLimits/Basic.html),
[official power documentation](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/Pow/Asymptotics.html)).
The closest existing repository result is
`Asymptotics.eventually_nat_floor_rpow_intermediate_bounds` in
`Analysis/Asymptotics/Scale/Power/IntermediateBlock.lean`: for $0<p<q$ it
gives $x^p\le\lfloor x^q\rfloor\le x^q$ eventually (and the sharper
$x^q-x^p\le\lfloor x^q\rfloor$ bound). That statement controls one rounded
block scale; it does not combine an independent sequence lower bound with a
product exponent budget. The new public result states precisely that
combination using only its natural real-sequence hypotheses, so it belongs in
the generic asymptotic-power layer rather than the N-selection or block-scale
layer.

The endpoint decomposition, sequence conversion, logarithmic scale module,
and all direct scale clients build successfully with the pinned toolchain.
Removing the transitive import also exposed `Cutoff.lean`'s use of
`Tendsto.rpow_const`; that file now imports Mathlib's power continuity module

## Cyclic-gap proof module boundary (2026-10-24)

`SparreAndersen/Composition/Lemmas/BlockProbability.lean` contains the
set-specific cyclic-block event, its inclusion--exclusion reduction, and the
factorization over the cyclic gaps. The event and the two statements consumed
by `Composition/CyclicGapSum.lean` remain proof-chain declarations under
`Lemmas/`: their hypotheses and conclusions are tied to the selected cyclic
starts in the Bauer--Godrèche--Luck identity, with no separate clients. The
direct proof caller uses `import all` to access these non-public declarations;
the public cyclic-gap theorem imports its proof module privately. The remaining
event-geometry and measurability steps stay private. The helper module header
states their formulas and the exact source,
Bauer--Godrèche--Luck, Appendix A, equations (A.3)--(A.6) (DOI
10.1023/A:1004636216365; arXiv:cond-mat/9905252).

The abstraction check compared the pinned Mathlib API at revision
`380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51` and the repository's
`iidSequenceLaw_measure_forall_variableConsecutiveBlockEvent` in
`Probability/Sequence/IID/Blocks/Consecutive.lean`. Mathlib's
`Measure.pi_map_piCongrLeft` reindexes a finite product measure along an
equivalence, under sigma-finiteness; the repository theorem factors arbitrary
variable consecutive blocks under an IID sequence law. Both are more general
product-measure tools, but neither describes the particular event determined
by a finite set of cyclic starts and its wraparound gap. The helper therefore
stays with the cyclic-gap proof rather than being promoted as a thin API over
those results. See the [pinned Mathlib source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Constructions/Pi.lean#L745)
and [Mathlib documentation](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Constructions/Pi.html).

`Composition/CyclicGapSum.lean` and its downstream `Composition/Formula.lean`
build successfully with the pinned toolchain (3,137 Lake jobs).

finite-slot model no longer owns it.

380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51. Mathlib's

counts. It remains a separate bounded model; the countable-offspring speed

## Extended-real sequence limits used by Kingman (2026-10-24)

The real-sequence-to-`EReal` translation and perturbation facts were previously
declared publicly inside `Probability/Ergodic/Kingman/Companion.lean` and
`Derriennic.lean`, although their statements require no probability or
ergodicity. They now form one reusable family in
`Order/EReal/LiminfLimsup.lean`, with arbitrary index type and nontrivial
filter: translation by a finite real constant commutes with limsup and liminf;
a difference tending to zero preserves either extended-real limit; and a
convergent additive real term contributes its finite limit. The EReal
translation order isomorphism is also stated at this owner.

The abstraction check used Mathlib's generic `OrderIso.limsup_apply` and its
liminf dual, plus `EReal.addLECancellable_coe` from the pinned source at
`Vendor/Mathlib/Mathlib/Order/LiminfLimsup.lean` and
`Vendor/Mathlib/Mathlib/Data/EReal/Operations.lean`. Mathlib provides the
order-isomorphism transport and the EReal addition cancellation separately,

## Lévy–Khintchine proof support and citation review (2026-10-25)

`LevyKhintchine/Truncation.lean` contained only the radius-one small-jump set,
the radius-`ε` large-jump set, and their membership, measurability, complement,
and monotonicity facts. These names occur throughout the internal representation
and semigroup proof chain, but none appears in a public theorem statement; the
pinned Mathlib tree provides the general set and metric-ball operations rather
than this Lévy-specific notation. The group is now in
`LevyKhintchine/Lemmas/JumpRegions.lean` and is imported with `import all` by
proof clients. This is one shared, coherent proof-support module, not a separate
file for each elementary fact. Publicly useful constructions and results remain
at `LevyKhintchine/` and `LevyKhintchine/Semigroup/`.

The article-level representation and converse now identify Sato, *Lévy
Processes and Infinitely Divisible Distributions*, Cambridge Studies in
Advanced Mathematics 68, Cambridge University Press (1999), Theorem 8.1, and
state the open-unit-ball truncation convention. The uniqueness module names the
same theorem and full bibliographic source; the title and edition are listed in
the publisher's official [Cambridge front matter](https://assets.cambridge.org/97805215/53025/frontmatter/9780521553025_frontmatter.pdf)
and the author's [bibliography](https://www.ksato.jp/). The organization follows
Mathlib's guidance that module documentation describe the theory and intended
use of a file, with module and declaration names reflecting mathematical
content; it gives no one-lemma-per-file rule ([Mathlib style guide](https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/style.html),
[Mathlib naming guide](https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/naming.html)).

The moved support module, its representation and semigroup clients, and the
representation entry point build successfully with the pinned toolchain.

The canonical first-order jump displacement `h(x)=x 1_{|x|<1}` was also
reviewed against its clients in the stable jump model, Poisson characteristic
functions, and finite-variation Lévy theory. It is now defined with its
integrability theorem in `MeasureTheory/Measure/Levy/Cutoff.lean`;
`LevyKhintchine/FiniteVariation.lean` retains the complex compensation and
uncompensated-integrand identities. Literature search found the natural general
notion of a truncation function: bounded `h : ℝᵈ → ℝᵈ` equal to the identity
near zero, with `x 1_D(x)` as the canonical example (Baurdoux and
Papapantoleon, *An Introduction to Lévy Processes*, §5, Definition 5.6 and
Example 5.9(i), [lecture notes](https://actuarweb.aegean.gr/levy2019/uploads/1/1/5/5/115582233/baurdoux_papapantoleon_levyprocesses.pdf)).
The present triple and exponent fix the unit canonical cutoff, and the current
clients share that convention. A general-`h` representation would require
parameterizing the triple, exponent, drift conversion, and uniqueness API, so
the shared map belongs at the Lévy-measure cutoff layer while the full general
interface remains outside the current formalization scope.

## Stable random-walk path-law escape-rate ownership (2026-10-25)

`exists_generatedStableProcess_escapeRate_of_tightSource` previously lived in
`Probability/Process/RandomWalk/SmallDeviation/Mogulskii/Stable/Discrete/FromIncrementLaw/Path/Law.lean`.
Its hypotheses are a zero-centered stable domain-of-attraction limit, tightness
of normalized random-walk path laws, and a nontrivial sign probability at zero;
its conclusion constructs a stable clock path law and its tube escape rate.

assembly and by a finite-variance entrance estimate outside that subtree, so

process small deviations. The module and declaration now live at

under the functional-limit namespace, with no compatibility alias.

The standard stable functional-limit framework is stated by Embrechts,
Klüppelberg, and Mikosch, *Modelling Extremal Events for Insurance and
Finance*, Stochastic Modelling and Applied Probability 33, Springer (1997),
Chapter 3, Theorem 3.4.2, DOI 10.1007/978-3-642-33483-2. That theorem supplies
the surrounding invariance-principle context; this Lean result keeps
tightness explicit and obtains the escape rate by composing the repository's
stable path-law construction with its path-law escape-rate transfer.

liminf part of Proposition 3.3 in Anders Karlsson's Chapter 12, and its
statement applies to every finite measure-preserving system and integrable
subadditive cocycle satisfying the stated lower bound. It is now exposed at
`Kingman/EnvelopeInvariant.lean` as a complete theorem; the pointwise shifted-
sequence comparison has one caller and remains a private lemma in that file.

stage rather than one small helper. This placement agrees with the source
proof and avoids a separate module for a single short comparison.

limit APIs used by this proof, but no subadditive-cocycle liminf-invariance
result was found in `Mathlib/Probability/Ergodic`. The published source states
this invariance as Proposition 3.3, so this local Kingman theorem is retained
at the subject level ([Karlsson, Chapter 12, Proposition 3.3](https://www.unige.ch/math/folks/karlsson/subaddnew.pdf); [published chapter](https://doi.org/10.1017/9781316576571.014)).

## Branching-cloud slice order (2026-10-25)

Reviewed `Combinatorics/BranchingWalk/Cloud/Order`. The six existing modules
form a coherent interface: `Slice` defines the lower-tail measure order and
rankwise order on one cloud slice; `Basic` lifts the slice relation to every
time; `DominatingMap` carries an injective comparison between labelled sets;
`SliceDominatingMap` specializes that map to cloud particles; and `Selection`
and `DynamicSelection` prove the rankwise and dynamically ordered first-`N`
consequences. The public concepts have distinct statements, and the source
structure has no redundant standalone proof files. The module headers already
describe each public declaration with its mathematical content; I standardized
their headings to `## Public declarations`.

The order comparison is the lower-tail convention used in the project source;
the cited Bérard--Gouéré paper writes the equivalent upper-tail comparison.
The two orientations are derived by passing to the order dual while retaining
the same source/target cloud order. Mathlib's pinned `OrderEmbedding` maps
between ordered types while preserving and reflecting their order; it does
not express an injection between unrelated label types whose separate score
functions satisfy `targetScore (f a) ≤ sourceScore a`. The local
`Cloud.DominatingMap` therefore remains a complete generic labelled-set
construction at the cloud-order boundary, with the cloud-specific slice map
as its specialization ([Mathlib order-embedding API](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Order/Hom/Basic.html); [Bérard--Gouéré, Section 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/0811.2782)).

The six cloud-order modules and their selection/coupling clients build with
the pinned toolchain (3,287 Lake jobs), and `git diff --check` passes. The
earlier production scan reported 1,559 modules, 738 declaration inventories,

nonempty finite integer family of diameter at most $w$ into $[0,w]$;

finite family of uniform corridors; `Corridor` gives the corresponding

## Order-topological floor, limit, and interval-time interfaces (2026-10-25)

Reviewed `Topology/Order/FloorCadlag.lean`, `Topology/Order/Limit.lean`, and
`Topology/Order/UnitInterval/Time.lean`. The floor module gives càdlàg
regularity for both $x\mapsto\lfloor x\rfloor$ and
$x\mapsto\lfloor x\rfloor_+$. The limit module proves a two-index squeeze:
for each fixed approximant index, eventual lower and upper bounds converge
along the original filter, and the limits of those bounds converge to $L$;
then the bounded function converges to $L$. The interval-time module supplies
the affine surjectivity statements and a named identity clock used in process
clock interfaces.

The unit-interval coordinate was duplicated locally under an uppercase
`UnitInterval` namespace. The pinned Mathlib module already defines
`unitInterval.toNNReal`, its continuity theorem, endpoint values, and the
coercion formula. The local duplicate and its continuity/range wrappers have
been removed; call sites now use the Mathlib coordinate directly. This module
retains the additional affine-parametrization results and the semantically
named clock. The former terminal-coordinate simp wrapper was removed after
confirming that it had no clients and restated Mathlib's
`unitInterval.toNNReal_one` for the equivalent top notation. The pinned source is
`Vendor/Mathlib/Mathlib/Topology/UnitInterval.lean` at revision
`380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51` ([Mathlib UnitInterval API](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Topology/UnitInterval.html)).

Mathlib's `Filter.Tendsto.squeeze` applies when the lower and upper functions
converge to the same limit along the same filter. The local two-index result
uses a separate approximant index and only requires eventual bounds after an
index is fixed, so it is a genuine extension of that API rather than a second
statement of the same-index squeeze theorem ([pinned Mathlib source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51/Mathlib/Topology/Order/Basic.lean), [official API docs](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Topology/Order/Basic.html)).
Mathlib has no `IsCadlag` floor instances; the two floor theorems remain in
`Topology/Order` as deterministic order-topology facts that provide the
standard examples used by path representations.

## General filter limits and slow diagonal selection (2026-10-25)

Reviewed the two modules directly under `Order/Filter`. `LiminfLimsup` groups
the bounded-real limsup and liminf invariance statements under the same
vanishing-perturbation hypothesis. `SlowDiagonal` contains one general
selector: from $\forall k,\;P(k,n)$ eventually for each fixed $k$, it
constructs a monotone $d_n\to\infty$ such that $P(d_n,n)$ eventually. The
selector is a standalone public result because it states a general
order/filter construction independently of an asymptotic scale. The
scale-level wrapper applies it to quantitative errors, and the regular-
variation slow-scale construction consumes that wrapper. The scale-specific
error bound remains in `Analysis/Asymptotics/Scale/SlowDiagonal`.

This split follows Mathlib's module-location review criteria: declarations may
be placed in a focused file when that gives clients a smaller import, and a
file is split when it covers multiple topics or becomes too long. Thus a
single theorem can justify its own file when it names a distinct reusable
construction and keeps its dependency boundary focused; a one-use calculation
that only advances an owning theorem remains private or under that owner's
`Lemmas/` subtree. See the [Mathlib pull request review guide's location
criteria](https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/pr-review.html#location-location).
The pinned `Mathlib/Order/Filter/AtTopBot/Basic.lean` API supplies the
eventual-at-top threshold interface used by the construction, while a search
of the pinned `Mathlib/Order/Filter`, `Mathlib/Topology`, and
`Mathlib/Analysis` sources found no equivalent selector theorem
([pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51/Mathlib/Order/Filter/AtTopBot/Basic.lean),
[official API documentation](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Order/Filter/AtTopBot/Basic.html)).

## Continuous-log uniqueness uses the Mathlib covering-map API (2026-10-25)

The continuous-log uniqueness argument in `LevyKhintchine/Uniqueness.lean`
was also used by two stable-exponent theorems. A focused search of the pinned
Mathlib source found a more general result: `IsCoveringMap.eq_of_comp_eq`
proves equality of continuous lifts over any preconnected domain when the
lifts agree at one point. Mathlib also provides
`Complex.isCoveringMap_exp`, viewing the complex exponential as a covering map
onto the nonzero complex numbers. The Lévy--Khintchine and stable-exponent
proofs now apply these interfaces directly, converting equality of complex
exponentials to equality in the nonzero-complex subtype.

This is the appropriate abstraction boundary: the local clients consume
Mathlib's generic covering-map uniqueness theorem directly, without adding a
specialized corollary. Mathlib groups related logarithm-branch results by
topic in `Analysis/Complex/BranchLogRoot.lean` and exponential properties by
topic in `Analysis/SpecialFunctions/Exp.lean`, which supports concept-based
modules rather than one file per corollary.

## Finite-measure support modules (2026-10-26)

Reviewed `Measure/Finite/{AtomFiniteness,Partition,OnFamily,Domination}.lean`
as one coherent subject grouping. `AtomFiniteness` covers the implication
$\sum_i w_i<\infty\Rightarrow\{i:c\le w_i\}\text{ is finite}$ and the
resulting existence of a minimum when real sublevel sets are finite.
`Partition` gives a complete finite disjoint-cell inequality:
if $\mu(A_i\cap B_i)=\mu(A_i)\mu(B_i)$ and $\mu(B_i)\ge c$, then
$c\mu(\bigcup_i A_i)\le\mu(\bigcup_i(A_i\cap B_i))$. These results have
independent statements at the level of summable weights and arbitrary
measures; `Partition` requires neither independence nor a probability
normalization. They are complete reusable conclusions, so their standalone
modules are appropriate even though one exposes a single main inequality.
The intermediate subset form in `AtomFiniteness` is documented as support
for its threshold-set result rather than as a separate subject entry.

Compared against the pinned Mathlib source, the summable-weight argument uses
Mathlib's `ENNReal.tendsto_cofinite_zero_of_tsum_ne_top`; the local result
extracts its finite-threshold-set consequence. The finite-family API already
uses Mathlib's `IsFiniteMeasureOnCompacts` for compact sets, while its
one-sided ray families and the a.e. domination theorem add the stated
family-wide interfaces. The partition result is derived from Mathlib's
null-measurable finite-union measure formula and `ENNReal` sum inequalities.
Added formula-bearing inventories to `AtomFiniteness` and `Partition`, and
expanded their ownership-map entry. The four modules and their inspected
clients build successfully (2,414 Lake jobs).

## General block-path range limit and stable specialization (2026-10-26)

The closed-range limsup estimate formerly declared in
`Mogulskii/Stable/Corridor.lean` used only weak convergence, positive scaling,
the deterministic range-to-open-tube inclusion, and an almost-sure zero
start. Its stable-process-law hypothesis supplied only that last property.
Generalized it to arbitrary measurable source spaces, path-valued random
variables, and zero-start limiting laws, and initially placed it in
`Probability/ConvergenceInDistribution/SkorokhodRange.lean`: for a path law
converging to the law of `cX`, with `c>0`, the
range-oscillation bound `w∈ℝ`, and margin `δ>0`,
\[
\limsup_n\mathbb P(X_n\in\{\operatorname{osc}\le w\})
\le \mathbb P(X(0)=0,\ \operatorname{osc}(X)<(w+\delta)/c).
\]
The public theorem is a complete result at the weak-convergence/range-event
interface, rather than a block-specific helper. It uses Mathlib's closed-set
Portmanteau estimate, then proves the scaling and margin inclusion. The pinned
Mathlib revision is
`380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51`; its
[`MeasureTheory.Measure.Portmanteau` API](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Measure/Portmanteau.html)
provides the general closed-set limsup implication, while the path-set and
scale geometry supply the additional conclusion here. The stable Mogulskii
module now keeps only the one-block IID event bridge and exponential block
estimates; it obtains the zero-start condition from the stable path law and
calls the general result. Removed the block-specific wrapper and updated
the axiom-check source to the new public name, without a compatibility alias.

`ν (g ⁻¹' s) ≤ μ (f ⁻¹' s)`. `Tail.lean` now proves the real upper-tail form by
specializing to `Set.Ici threshold`; it remains a separate semantic entry,
while the generic event transfer is owned by `Order.lean`. `Basic.lean` now
lists its joint-law constructors and coordinate operations in its module
header.

The abstraction check used the pinned Mathlib APIs
`IsUpperSet` in `Mathlib/Order/UpperLower/Basic.lean` and
`measure_mono_ae` in `Mathlib/MeasureTheory/OuterMeasure/AE.lean`, at revision
`380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51`. The pinned source supplies upper
sets, measurable preimages, marginal pushforwards, and a.e. measure
monotonicity, but no coupling-level preimage comparison combining them. The
new theorem keeps only the order, measurability, and marginal assumptions
needed by its meaning. No compatibility alias was added. The coupling modules
and `BranchingRandomWalk/Coupling/Slice.lean` build, the import-boundary checker
passes, and `git diff --check` passes.

## Real-distribution and finite-product interfaces (2026-10-26)

Standardized the declaration inventories in `Probability/Distributions/
{Rademacher,Scaling}.lean` and `Probability/MeasureTheory/FiniteProduct.lean`.
The Rademacher module groups its two-point probability law with the Boolean
encoding, pushforward identity, integral formula, and unit truncated second
moment. `FiniteProduct.lean` keeps the two reverse logarithmic comparisons
together because they are the same ENNReal-to-real conversion under opposite
product bounds. The single theorem in `Scaling.lean` remains a standalone
module because it states the complete distribution-level scaling law and
does not depend on a particular random-walk or named distribution.

The scaling result is now `ProbabilityTheory.cdf_map_mul`, with arbitrary
threshold $x$: for $r>0$,
$\operatorname{cdf}((y\mapsto ry)_*\mu)(x)=\operatorname{cdf}(\mu)(x/r)$.
This is the inverse-image identity for $(-\infty,x]$ under positive
multiplication. The pinned Mathlib CDF module provides `cdf_eq_real`, and
Mathlib's measure-map module provides the pushforward API, but neither states
this threshold-rescaling formula; see the [official CDF API](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Probability/CDF.html),
the [official measure-map API](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Measure/Map.html),
and the [pinned CDF source](https://github.com/maix00/mathlib4/blob/380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51/Mathlib/Probability/CDF.lean).
The seven stable-Mogul'skii clients now use the general theorem at $x=0$;
there is no compatibility alias for the former zero-only statement. The
scaling module and all three affected client files compile with the pinned
toolchain; existing `letI` style warnings in the clients remain unrelated.

## Internal lemma declaration and additive-path abstraction review (2026-10-26)

the affected probability and additive-path areas. The three floor-index

checkout at revision `380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51`; the official
API documents the result for arbitrary seminormed additive commutative groups
at <https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Analysis/Normed/Group/Basic.html>.

`exists_finset_Icc_cover_inside` remains an internal lemma under the Mogul'skii
partition proof. It adds the two inner endpoints to a finite net so that the
whole outer interval is covered by balls of the margin radius whose centers

## Cyclic-gap proof-stage organization (2026-10-26)

Split the 874-line `Composition/Lemmas/BlockProbability.lean` proof chain into
`Composition/Lemmas/BlockProbability/{Event,Measure,IIDFactorization}.lean`.
`Event.lean` defines the selected cyclic adjacent-block event and proves its
equivalence and measurability; `Measure.lean` substitutes that event into the
finite inclusion--exclusion identity and identifies it with survival on the
cyclic gaps; `IIDFactorization.lean` factors the finite IID product measure
over those gaps. This follows the separate equations (A.4), (A.5), and (A.6)
in Appendix A of Bauer, Godrèche, and Luck, “Statistics of persistent events
in the binomial random walk: Will the drunken sailor hit the sober man?”
(*Journal of Statistical Physics* 96 (1999), 963--1019, DOI
10.1023/A:1004636216365, arXiv:cond-mat/9905252).

The adjacent-block event remains under `Lemmas/`: it is indexed by the
selected cyclic starts and exists only to prove this composition identity.
Only helpers needed across these proof stages are module-visible `lemma` or
`def` declarations; the event decomposition, IID factorization, and the
principal cyclic-gap identity remain in their existing subject and entry
modules. Removed the unused positive-horizon hypotheses from the event
equivalence and probability-factorization helpers. The three helper stages
and `Composition/CyclicGapSum.lean` compile successfully with the pinned
toolchain (3,137 Lake jobs).

## Finite exponential-sum abstraction review (2026-10-26)

The endpoint-sublevel estimate and the positive-initial-mass capacity estimate
both turn two asymptotic rate bounds into a single exponential budget. Their
probability decompositions and rate calculations differ, but the shared
inequality is independent of those models: for finite nonempty $F$, if
$g\to+\infty$ and every exponent satisfies $e_i/g<c-\delta$ eventually for
one fixed $\delta>0$, then
\[
  \sum_{i\in F}\exp(e_i)\leq\exp(cg)
\]
eventually. The fixed factor $|F|$ is absorbed by the diverging margin
$\delta g$.

The pinned Mathlib revision
`380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51` has
[`ExpGrowth.expGrowthSup_sum`](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51/Mathlib/Analysis/Asymptotics/ExpGrowth.lean),
which says that the upper exponential growth of a finite ENNReal sum is the
maximum of the component growth rates under normalization by the natural-number
index. That API does not cover an arbitrary diverging scale or an indexed
family of real exponents. The repository's
`Analysis/Asymptotics/Sequence/LogSum.lean` instead studies logarithmic ratios
of positive sums at a denominator tending to $-\infty$; it does not state this
upper exponential-budget estimate. Therefore
`Analysis/Asymptotics/Sequence/ExponentialSum.lean` owns the reusable
uniform-gap result. The two probability modules now use it only for the final
finite-sum absorption; their model-specific hypotheses and estimates remain
with their current owners. Targeted builds of the new module and both clients
passed.

## Power-bounded logarithmic count review (2026-10-26)

The cubic-scale estimate for $\log(u+1)/L\to0$ appeared twice: once as a
private helper in the endpoint-sublevel module and once as a theorem-specific
helper in the drawdown-spine proof chain. Both instances used only
$u/L^3\to t>0$. The reusable statement needs less: for any filter, if
$L\to+\infty$, $u\geq0$, $C\geq0$, $p>0$, and $u\leq C L^p$ eventually,
then $\log(u+1)/L\to0$. This now lives in
`Analysis/Asymptotics/Sequence/LogarithmicScale.lean`; the two call sites
derive the required eventual power bound from their scale limits. The duplicate
cubic helper was removed, with no alias retained.

The pinned Mathlib revision
`380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51` provides
[`Real.isLittleO_log_id_atTop`](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51/Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/Log/Basic.lean)
and the negative-power limit in
[`Pow.Asymptotics`](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/380f2aafb622cb2c1c93dac545b6389083c68c51/Mathlib/Analysis/SpecialFunctions/Pow/Asymptotics.lean),
but no combined logarithmic estimate under an eventual power bound. The new
module uses those standard limits and states the general order bound needed by
both clients. Targeted builds of the new module, the drawdown-spine proof
modules, and the endpoint-sublevel module passed.

## Finite-variance positivity parameter and Spitzer condition (2026-10-27)

Reviewed `Probability/Process/RandomWalk/Fluctuation/FiniteVarianceSignLimit.lean`.
Its three statements are complete probability limits for a centered
finite-variance IID walk: positive partial sums converge in probability to
mass $1/2$, their Cesàro averages satisfy Spitzer's condition with parameter
$1/2$, and the nonnegative endpoint convention also converges to mass $1/2$.
All three belong at the random-walk fluctuation layer: the first and third
are the strict and non-strict Gaussian half-line limits, and the second is
the corresponding ladder-epoch input. The module has no one-use theorem
fragments to extract; its proof already specializes the normal-domain
attraction and null-frontier Portmanteau results.

The sources are identified precisely in the module: R. A. Doney,
*Spitzer's condition and ladder variables in random walks*, Theorem 2 and
condition (1), *Probability Theory and Related Fields* 101 (1995), 577--580,
DOI 10.1007/BF01202785; and M. Bauer, C. Godrèche, and J.-M. Luck,
*Statistics of persistent events in the binomial random walk: Will the
drunken sailor hit the sober man?*, Appendix A, equations (A.1)--(A.3),
DOI 10.1023/A:1004636216365. The primary texts were checked at the [Doney
DOI record](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01202785) and the [Bauer--Godrèche--Luck
arXiv record](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/9905252). The pinned Mathlib
source has the general normal-domain, Gaussian half-line, and Portmanteau
interfaces used here, but no random-walk positivity-parameter or Spitzer
condition statement.

The declaration signatures expose `IsCenteredSecondMoment`,
`iidSequenceLaw`, and `AdditivePath.displacement`. Accordingly,
`Moments.Real`, `Sequence.IID.Basic`, and `AdditivePath.Basic` are the public

modules occur only in proof bodies and are now ordinary imports. The module
build completed successfully (3,361 Lake jobs); an importer with only this
public module checked all three public signatures. The cross-repository

module, citation, and abstraction audit remains open.

## `Lemmas/` visibility and importer audit (2026-10-27)

The production tree contains 162 modules below a `Lemmas/` path. All use the
new module system, none opens an `@[expose] public section`, none uses a
`public import`, and all production clients that import one use `import all`.
This confirms the package-private visibility and import convention required
by `lean/ARCHITECTURE.md`; it does not establish that each lemma is at the
right semantic layer or is still needed.

One module has no production importer:
`Mogulskii/Stable/Discrete/Bridge/Lemmas/TerminalLeftDecay.lean`. Its support
modules `EndpointCorridorDecay.lean` and `TerminalLeftAsymptotics.lean` are
also used only by that chain, while the axiom-check source
`BranchingProcessTest/Mogulskii/Stable/Discrete/Bridge/TerminalLeftDecay.lean`
imports it for declaration checks. The current proof route records this as a
standalone formalization of the equation-(34) comparison in Mogul'skii's
Theorem 3, Section 4; it is outside the import closure of the repository's
`Mogulskii/Theorems.lean` entry and its finite-partition theorem assembly.
The chain is specialized to that cited comparison, so its estimates remain in
the package-private `Bridge/Lemmas/` subtree rather than becoming general
stable-process APIs. These six modules separate the event definitions, finite
bridge comparison and geometry, endpoint decay, logarithmic transfer, and
final assembly; their current sizes (64, 370, 212, 214, 117, and 352 lines,
respectively, including `Events.lean`) make this a proof chain rather than a
single short lemma worth inlining. Keep this supplementary source-result
formalization distinct from the main theorem route; this review does not claim
that the main entry currently derives its result through equation (34). This
split is based on proof stages and import boundaries, not a rule that each
lemma needs its own file: Mathlib's [location review guidance](https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/pr-review.html#location-location)
asks whether files should split when they become very long (for example,

## Analytic capacity interface review (2026-10-27)

Reviewed the four modules under `MeasureTheory/Analytic/Capacity/`. They form
a public mathematical interface rather than a collection of theorem-specific
proof steps: `Basic.lean` defines capacities and capacitable sets;
`CountableClosure.lean` proves the general countable-paving closure estimate;
`Projection.lean` transports capacities and capacitability through
projections; and `Choquet.lean` derives the Choquet theorem and the analytic
set null-measurability consequences. The sequence-selection construction
inside `CountableClosure.lean` and the single-use preimage closure argument in
`Projection.lean` are private. The one downstream path-corridor client uses
the resulting analytic-measurability interface, while the capacity axioms
and projection theorem apply to arbitrary set families and compact systems;
they therefore remain at the reusable `MeasureTheory/Analytic/Capacity/`
level, with no additional `Lemmas/` directory.

The pinned Mathlib source tree defines `AnalyticSet` and proves that Borel
sets are analytic and that continuous images of analytic sets remain analytic
in `Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Constructions/Polish/Basic.lean`. It does not provide
the paving-analytic predicate, abstract capacities, or Choquet capacitability.
Thus the paving and capacity declarations fill a general measure-theoretic
gap. The former local `MeasureTheory/Analytic/Projection.lean` only renamed
Mathlib's continuous-image result and had no clients, so it was removed rather
than retained as a wrapper.
The module namespace remains `MeasureTheory.Analytic.Paving`: capacities are
parameterized by the set family `p`, and capacitability is defined using its
countable closure operations; the sibling `Paving` modules own those closure
operations and the analytic-set predicate. The citations identify He,
Wang, and Yan's Theorems 1.34--1.35 and Bichteler's Theorem A.5.8(ii).

The adjacent `MeasureTheory/Analytic/Paving/Lemmas/FiniteUnion.lean` contains
one shared conversion from the project-wide finite-set characterization of
`supClosure` to the `ℕ`-indexed finite-union representation required by both
the paving and capacity projection proofs. Keeping this substantial,
two-client adapter in `Lemmas/` avoids promoting a proof representation to a
public API. The general antitone-intersection projection theorem stays in
`Paving/Projection.lean`, where both clients can use it. `Paving/Analytic/`
keeps the separate analytic-set definitions, closure operations,
measurability, and projection interfaces; this review found no competing
entry module or misplaced helper in that family. The four capacity modules
and their downstream `StepCorridor.NullMeasurable` client build successfully
(2,841 Lake jobs); an explicit build of all seven paving and four capacity
modules also succeeds (2,007 Lake jobs).

## Finite-sum and additive-path interface review (2026-10-27)

Reviewed the seven modules under `Algebra/BigOperators/` and
`Algebra/Order/BigOperators/` against their production clients and the pinned
Mathlib API. Mathlib owns `Fin.partialSum`, `Fin.finCycle`, finite-sum
reindexing, and the ordered-sum comparison primitives used in these proofs.
The local `AdditivePath` interface packages accumulated increments and finite
path prefixes without probability assumptions; `PartialSum` states endpoint
and cyclic-rotation identities; `CyclicReindex` relates Mathlib's
`Fin.finCycle` permutation to those path sums. These are mathematical
interfaces used across random walks, branching walks, Brownian grids, and
finite-state estimates, so they remain at the algebraic owner rather than
under a theorem-specific `Lemmas/` tree. The module layout has no same-parent
name collisions and no proof-only `Lemmas/` candidates. The continuous
finite-partial-sum map in `Topology/Algebra/BigOperators/PartialSum.lean`
complements `MeasureTheory/Function/FinPartialSum.lean`: the former assumes
continuous addition and proves continuity, while the latter assumes measurable
addition and proves measurability. Both reuse Mathlib's `Fin.partialSum`
without duplicating its definition. The topology module's recovered ledger row
was checked against the current source and rebuilt directly (1,287 Lake jobs).

The three weighted-sum comparison theorems have production clients in the
finite-state eigenfunction and Rademacher survival arguments. Their earlier
`\mathbb R`-only statements were narrower than those arguments require; the
unscaled comparison now assumes an ordered commutative ring, while the two
quotient comparisons assume an ordered field. The sibling normalization
identities are also expressed over an arbitrary field. No exact named
normalized-weighted-sum identity was found in the pinned Mathlib source; its
finite-sum API supplies the underlying `sum_div`, `mul_sum`, and order
monotonicity operations ([Mathlib finite-sum API](https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/Algebra/BigOperators/Ring/Finset.html)).
The normalization module is kept as a coherent generic algebraic interface,
not as a one-use proof file; it currently has no production callers.

Proof-route review checked each declaration against its Lean proof. The path
and block identities reduce to finite-sum recurrences, interval reindexing,
and the stated algebraic assumptions. The cyclic nonnegativity result chooses
a minimum among the finitely many preterminal path values; before the minimum,
the rotated path is a difference from that minimum, and after the wrap it is
the nonnegative terminal displacement plus such a difference. This is the
finite-path argument used to show the event decomposition following (A.3) in
Bauer, Godrèche, and Luck, *Statistics of persistent events in the binomial
random walk: Will the drunken sailor hit the sober man?*, Appendix A,
*Journal of Statistical Physics* 96 (1999), 963--1019,
[arXiv:cond-mat/9905252](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/9905252). The precise
claim is the event covering in the paragraph after (A.3); the Lean theorem
states its deterministic finite-path core for linearly ordered additive
groups. The remaining algebraic identities are direct finite-sum facts and do
not invoke an external proof.

The seven owners and their production clients build successfully with the
pinned toolchain (3,138 Lake jobs). Placement, abstraction, proof-route, and
citation review are complete for these seven modules. This is a local subtree
review; the remaining library-wide semantic and citation audit is still open.
